title: California PERB Decision No. 3018E
summary: Description: David Ferrer primarily alleged that Downey Unified School District interfered with protected activities and retaliated against him for such activities. In a fifth amended charge, Ferrer withdrew his earlier allegations and instead alleged for the first time that the District had retaliated against and interfered with protected activities by suing him in retaliation for pursuing earlier versions of his charge. PERB’s Office of the General Counsel (OGC) dismissed the fifth amended charge on two grounds. First, OGC found that the charge could not proceed because Ferrer was not a District employee when the District sued him. In the alternative, OGC found that Ferrer’s charge did not state a prima facie case of interference or retaliation because the facts Ferrer had alleged would not establish that the District’s lawsuit both lacked a reasonable basis and was filed for an unlawful purpose. Ferrer appealed. Disposition: The Board affirmed OGC’s dismissal. First, the Board held that an employee’s post‑separation allegations are actionable if they are integrally tied to the employment relationship and satisfy all other substantive and procedural requirements. For an employee’s charge against an employer, “integrally tied” normally requires that the post-separation conduct arise directly from the employment relationship or its termination. (See, e.g., Hartnell Community College District , supra , PERB Decision No. 2452, pp. 30-33.) When the respondent is a union, “integrally tied” normally requires that the post-separation conduct directly involves the union’s acts or omissions in a matter in which it owes the employee a duty of fair representation. (See, e.g., SEIU (Lacy) (2016) PERB Decision No. 2486-M, adopting proposed decision at pp. 4-7.) The Board was not required to decide whether Ferrer sufficiently alleged that the District’s lawsuit was integrally tied to his employment relationship, for the Board affirmed OGC’s dismissal on the alternate ground.
text:
STATE OF CALIFORNIA
DECISION OF THE
PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS BOARD
DAVID FERRER,
Charging Party, Case No. LA-CE-6977-E
v. PERB Decision No. 3018
DOWNEY UNIFIED SCHOOL DISTRICT,
April 24, 2026
Respondent.
Appearances: David Ferrer, on his own behalf; Dannis Woliver Kelley by Candace M.
Bandoian and Noah M. Rosen, Attorneys, for Downey Unified School District.
Before Banks, Chair; Krantz and Paulson, Members.
DECISION
KRANTZ, Member: This case is before the Public Employment Relations Board
(PERB or Board) on appeal by Charging Party David Ferrer from a determination by
PERB’s Office of the General Counsel (OGC) to dismiss his unfair practice charge.
Ferrer primarily alleges that Respondent Downey Unified School District violated the
Educational Employment Relations Act (EERA) by interfering with protected activities
and retaliating against him for such activities.1
After reviewing Ferrer’s initial charge and four subsequent amended charges,
OGC issued Ferrer a warning letter. The letter explained that Ferrer’s charge was
untimely and did not include allegations that would, if proven, establish an EERA
violation. The warning letter afforded Ferrer an opportunity to amend his charge and
1 EERA is codified at Government Code section 3540 et seq. All statutory
references are to the Government Code.

thereby attempt to cure its deficiencies. Ferrer took advantage of this opportunity,
filing a fifth amended charge. In that filing, Ferrer withdrew his earlier allegations and
instead alleged for the first time that the District had retaliated against and interfered
with protected activities by suing him in retaliation for pursuing earlier versions of his
charge.
OGC dismissed the fifth amended charge on two grounds. First, citing San
Francisco Unified School District (2009) PERB Decision No. 2000, OGC found that
Ferrer’s fifth amended charge could not proceed because he was not a District
employee when the District sued him. In the alternative, OGC found that Ferrer’s
charge does not state a prima facie case of interference or retaliation. Regarding this
latter conclusion, OGC explained that the facts Ferrer had alleged would not establish
that the District’s lawsuit both lacked a reasonable basis and was filed for an unlawful
purpose. (See, e.g., Operating Engineers Local Union No. 3, AFL-CIO (Wagner et al.)
(2021) PERB Decision No. 2782-M, pp. 8-10 (Operating Engineers) [PERB applies a
qualified litigation privilege based on the principles first set forth in Bill Johnson’s
Restaurants, Inc. v. National Labor Relations Bd. (1983) 461 U.S. 731, requiring a
charging party to show that allegedly unlawful litigation lacked a reasonable basis and
was filed for an unlawful purpose].)
Ferrer appealed OGC’s dismissal.
DISCUSSION
Under EERA section 3541.5(a) and comparable provisions in other
PERB-administered laws, an “employee, employee organization, or employer” may file
an unfair practice charge. The laws we administer are not alone in failing to state
2

whether employees’ right to pursue a claim includes the right of former employees to
challenge alleged adverse actions occurring after their separation from employment.
The issue arises in rare cases like this one, where an employer acts against a former
employee after separation.
In Robinson v. Shell Oil Co. (1997) 519 U.S. 337 (Robinson), the Supreme
Court unanimously held that “employees,” as used in Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of
1964 (42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq.), includes former employees challenging
post-separation conduct. (Robinson, supra, 519 U.S. at p. 346.) The Court found it
immaterial that certain other federal statutes “have been more specific in their
coverage” of former employees. (Id. at pp. 341-342.) The Court emphasized that
Title VII contains no “temporal qualifier” limiting its protection to persons still employed
at the time of the alleged retaliation. (Id. at p. 341.) The same is true of the laws we
enforce.
In PERB cases brought by employees challenging post-separation conduct, our
precedent has been inconsistent. On the one hand, precedent normally does not bar
employees from pursuing charges against a union merely because the conduct at
issue occurred after the employees were no longer employed. (See, e.g., Service
Employees International Union United Healthcare Workers West (Lacy) (2016) PERB
Decision No. 2486-M, adopting proposed decision at pp. 4-7 (SEIU (Lacy)); but see
California Union of Safety Employees (Trevisanut, et al.) (1993) PERB Decision
No. 1029-S, p. 9 [charges against unions are limited to pre-separation acts].)
In PERB cases against employers, our precedent more commonly suggests
that charges must be limited to pre-separation acts. For instance, in San Francisco
3

Unified School District, supra, PERB Decision No. 2000, the Board stated that “a
charging party must have been an employee, employee organization, or employer at
the time of the alleged unfair practice.” (Id. at p. 3; see also, e.g., Monterey Peninsula
Community College District (2002) PERB Decision No. 1492, p. 2 [same]; but see
Hartnell Community College District (2015) PERB Decision No. 2452, pp. 30-33
(Hartnell) [EERA permits charge against employer for alleged post-termination failure
to pay charging party all amounts owed].)2
Although cases involving post-separation conduct more commonly arise against
union respondents given that unions often serve as gatekeepers to contractual
arbitration of termination grievances, there is no reason to apply a materially different
standard to post-separation conduct based on whether the respondent is a union or an
employer. Moreover, we find persuasive the Supreme Court’s reasoning in Robinson,
supra, 519 U.S. 337. Accordingly, we adjust our precedent and hold that an
employee’s post-separation allegations are actionable if they are integrally tied to the
employment relationship and satisfy all other substantive and procedural
requirements. For an employee’s charge against an employer, “integrally tied”
normally requires that the post-separation conduct arise directly from the employment
relationship or its termination. (See, e.g., Hartnell, supra, PERB Decision No. 2452,
pp. 30-33.) When the respondent is a union, “integrally tied” normally requires that the
2 Because the laws we enforce explicitly protect applicants for employment or
reemployment (see, e.g., EERA, § 3543.5(a)), there is no question that these laws bar
an employer from impeding a former employee's attempt to secure subsequent
employment, where such conduct constitutes retaliation for protected activity.
(Monterey Peninsula Unified School District (2017) PERB Decision No. 2530, pp. 7-8.)
Today’s decision does not impact that principle.
4

post-separation conduct directly involve the union’s acts or omissions in a matter in
which it owes the employee a duty of fair representation. (See, e.g., SEIU (Lacy),
supra, PERB Decision No. 2486-M, adopting proposed decision at pp. 4-7.)
This holding is also necessary because a categorical bar against charges that
challenge post-separation conduct would undercut fundamental labor law principles,
such as: (1) it is unlawful to retaliate against or interfere with the right to use PERB
processes (see Trustees of the California State University (East Bay) (2014) PERB
Decision No. 2391-H, p. 39 [remedying discrimination for using PERB processes is
“critical” to PERB’s “function of preserving those processes from abuse”]); and
(2) even when an employer has cause to issue discipline, it may not prospectively bar
employees from communicating with one another about such discipline or other
employment matters. (Claremont Unified School District (2019) PERB Decision
No. 2654, p. 11 & p.18, fn. 15 [noting that California’s public sector labor relations
laws contain “no more fundamental right” than the right to communicate with
coworkers, and finding employer acted unlawfully when, after issuing employee a
notice of intent to dismiss, it barred employee from contacting coworkers].)3
For these reasons, we partially overrule California Union of Safety Employees
(Trevisanut, et al.), supra, PERB Decision No. 1029-S, Monterey Peninsula
3 Moreover, PERB precedent recognizes that a union may pursue a charge
challenging employer conduct that tends to harm employee rights even when that
conduct is directed at an individual who lacks the right to file a charge, such as a
non-covered supervisor or manager. (State of California (Department of Consumer
Affairs) (2004) PERB Decision No. 1711-S, pp. 18-19.) This principle—that an unfair
practice charge does not necessarily turn on the status of the individual against whom
conduct is directed—further supports the conclusion that there is no categorical bar on
challenges to adverse actions occurring after an employee’s separation.
5

Community College District, supra, PERB Decision No. 1492, San Francisco Unified
School District, supra, PERB Decision No. 2000, and similar decisions to the extent
they can be interpreted as categorically barring all charging party employees from
challenging any conduct occurring after separation from employment. This change
does not alter any statutory provision identifying which individuals and entities can file
a charge; rather, it resolves a latent tension in our precedent by clarifying employees’
right to challenge post-separation conduct that is integrally tied to the employment
relationship.
In this case, we need not decide whether Ferrer has sufficiently alleged that the
District’s lawsuit was integrally tied to his employment relationship. That issue does
not affect the outcome because OGC correctly found that Ferrer’s allegations, if
proven, would not satisfy the standard set forth in Operating Engineers, supra, PERB
Decision No. 2782-M, pp. 8-10. According to the fifth amended charge, the District’s
lawsuit alleges that Ferrer violated a settlement agreement by pursuing his PERB
charge. Because the charge was protected activity, Ferrer has adequately alleged
facts that, if proven, would establish that the lawsuit constituted retaliation for
protected activity. However, Ferrer has not alleged facts that would show the lawsuit
was objectively baseless. We therefore affirm OGC’s dismissal of Ferrer’s charge.
ORDER
The amended unfair practice charge in Case No. LA-CE-6977-E is DISMISSED
WITHOUT LEAVE TO AMEND.
Chair Banks and Member Paulson joined in this Decision.
